title: ICRIR on the Troubles Bill: co-operation, powers, capacity and family engagement
label: 11 November 2026 · Troubles Bill follow-up
summary: The ICRIR’s leadership told the Committee that co-operation from the Republic of Ireland on legacy material remains stalled and will likely need a political solution tied to legislation in both jurisdictions. They welcomed some legal safeguards (an appeal against the Secretary of State on national security redactions) but raised concerns about other provisions such as the Attorney General consent clause and slow security checks. The commission says it is under-resourced for the likely caseload, has made strong progress on implementing Peter May’s recommendations, and stresses that careful, family-centred engagement and tailored reports are central to securing public confidence.

chapters.title: Co-operation with Ireland
chapters.takeaway: The ICRIR has had no substantive disclosure from the Republic of Ireland and says political agreement tied to both countries’ legislation is needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Sir Declan, since June have arrangements with the Irish Government on information-sharing improved?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: No. We've written about a dozen letters and got acknowledgements but no substantive replies. The crux is national security protections: in the UK the Secretary of State is guarantor and the Act creates strict rules we must follow.

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: We want the same kind of disclosure protocols with Ireland as we have with UK agencies, but matching their national-security protections is complex. That looks like a political issue that needs a political solution tied to legislation in both states.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You told us you made 11 requests to the Garda covering 31 deaths. Have you received any material?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: No substantive material. There have been acknowledgements, but the Garda told us they weren't in a position to provide information yet.

turns.speaker: Adam Jogee
turns.text: Why could Kenova engage with An Garda Síochána but ICRIR can’t?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Kenova was a policing criminal investigation under PSNI. ICRIR isn't a law-enforcement body, so it can’t send ILRs. If ILRs are needed they’d have to come from the Public Prosecution Service and only for cases that proceed criminally.

turns.speaker: Adam Jogee
turns.text: So until both legislatures act, significant cross-border information-sharing is unlikely?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Yes. Ireland is waiting to see the UK Bill; we would like synchronized implementation so the new commission can start with a clean slate.

chapters.title: Legal powers, national security and scrutiny
chapters.takeaway: The commission welcomes an appeal against the Secretary of State’s national security decisions, but concerns remain about AG consent for prosecutions and slow security checks.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: The Government added a clause requiring the Attorney General's consent for serious troubles prosecutions. What do you think?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Legally it shouldn't change outcomes compared with the PPS, but some will perceive it differently. It's a political choice and could be contentious.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: If Ireland's Oireachtas opposes that clause, could it harm co-operation?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Possibly. Governments may trade concessions; diplomacy will matter. I can't predict the political give-and-take.

turns.speaker: Sir Alec Shelbrooke
turns.text: You have the power to appeal a Secretary of State decision on national security—will you use it?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: We welcomed the right to appeal. We see the material and can judge public interest versus security. If misuse occurs—say to conceal embarrassment—we could challenge it in court, which should increase public confidence.

turns.speaker: Simon Hoare
turns.text: Might the right to appeal make the Secretary of State more cautious about over-using national security?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Yes. The appeal power itself should deter over-broad use and provide scrutiny, which could reassure sceptical people.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You’ve had long waits while the Secretary of State’s office carried out security checks—two months in one case. Is that avoidable?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Delays happen because agencies must be asked about security issues; if they don't respond quickly the 60-day window gets used. We need faster, clearer processes from agencies to avoid holding up publication.

chapters.title: Investigative workload and funding
chapters.takeaway: ICRIR is under-resourced for the likely caseload; they have submitted a business case and warn shortfall would shift pressure to costly public inquiries.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Amanda, do you have enough investigators and people to manage evidence and sensitivity tagging?

turns.speaker: Amanda Logan
turns.text: No. We need more staff. An independent review recommended about seven to nine syndicates—roughly 400 investigators and support—if AI is used; right now we have 189 operational staff, less than half what's needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would your amendment to shift sensitivity-marking away from PSNI reduce your workload?

turns.speaker: Amanda Logan
turns.text: Originators best know sensitivity, so their tagging helps. But if the commission must do all tagging, it is extra work; we'd need partnership with agencies to tag material accurately.

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: We currently have 159 investigations through eligibility, 57 in case support—over 200 active investigations. Some cases, like Warrenpoint or Guildford, are resource-heavy and can’t be handled with current staff.

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: We submitted a business case seeking £628 million to Treasury. That includes the current ringfenced £232 million and the costs of scaling up and running inquisitorial proceedings.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What have you spent so far and what if the business case is refused?

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: We’ve drawn down about £77m and spent about £64m to date, leaving £150–160m of the current allocation. If the business case fails, our capacity to scale up would be severely constrained and delivery would be impacted.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: Do you have an estimate of total cases coming?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Our central estimate is about 650 investigations over roughly seven and a half years. We aim for an average of 80–90 outcomes a year once fully scaled.

chapters.title: Peter May review and governance
chapters.takeaway: ICRIR has implemented most of Peter May’s 19 recommendations; three remain as business-as-usual actions, and cultural and financial controls have improved.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: You told us in June 11 of 19 May recommendations were done—what’s the update?

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: Significant progress: only three recommendations remain active. We've set up an independent-chaired finance committee, strengthened governance and sponsorship with the NIO, improved staff communications and recognised the union.

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: The three outstanding items are clarifying line management versus corporate centre roles, a formal lessons-learned project to run once enough cases reach reporting, and deeper understanding and headroom for AME budgeting.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: How are you checking cultural changes are working?

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: We use staff pulse surveys, union engagement, external consultants working with senior leadership and our joint oversight group with NIO to monitor and assure progress.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who in NIO do you engage with?

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: Different people for different functions, but the structured sponsorship committee is chaired by the NIO chief operating officer and provides formal oversight.

chapters.title: Reports, family engagement and publication
chapters.takeaway: ICRIR emphasises careful, personal engagement with families; reports may not publish every detail to protect safety or family concerns, and early outcomes can build public confidence.

turns.speaker: Chris Bloore
turns.text: You described the first September report as significant. When will more reports appear?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: We have one report published, one through the Secretary of State with criticisms that need a 30-day representations period and RI checks, so it won't appear before Christmas. In total we have nine completed investigations at varying stages; more will follow early next year.

turns.speaker: Chris Bloore
turns.text: Some criticism says your reports only re-review old material rather than find new lines. Is that fair?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Not entirely. Some cases won't yield new facts, but it still matters to families to know every stone was turned. Other investigations do produce new, meaningful information.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do families get more detail than the published report?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Often yes. We meet families during the process and give them information that might not appear in the public report—especially material withheld for security or because the family is worried about publication.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That concern about publication is strong for people living in Northern Ireland—are you tailoring reports for family safety?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Absolutely. Reports are family-centred and may omit or redact details that could put people at risk or cause serious distress, always balancing public interest and safety.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Finally, you want investigations and inquisitorial hearings better aligned—would that need legal tweaks?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Some practical tweaks might be needed. Our aim is to use investigative work to focus hearings only on what still needs examination, making proceedings more efficient and focused.
